Loved this game on the 360 and it's only better here........ if you do a couple things first. This game will only use one cpu core by default and as a result the frame rate will hitch and stutter as the cpu core is overloaded. While the game is running go to task manager, details, right click hot NFS11.exe, and select "affinity". Uncheck the CPU core in use, should be CPU0, and your other cores will take the processing load. Now you can enjoy whatever your GPU can handle. There are permanent ways to apply this tweak if you would like as this will have to be done every launch. I also would recommend forcing anti-aliasing and anisotropic filtering via nvcp or amd equivalent. Locking your frame rate is also a great way to even frame pacing and decrease input latency. Playing this game at 4k with 8Xmsaa, 16Xaf, and a silky stutter free framerate  gave my life meaning again. hope you enjoy.

To start off, I can't say that this is my favorite NFS game of all time, but it is certainly up there. I have been a NFS fan for a long time, dating back to the good old PS2 days with Most Wanted and Carbon. So far no other NFS game, in my opinion, has been better than those, but Hot Pursuit is still a lot of fun, and here's why.

[b]PROS:[/b]

The graphics are fantastic. The car models are awesome as always, and the scenery is beautiful. Yes, scenery especially matters to me because I want to be able to go for a nice drive, if that's what I'm in the mood for. It looks great at 200+ MPH too! Now don't expect Metro: Last Light graphics, but it really is a nice looking game.

There are quite a few cars as well. I can't say for sure how many there are, but it's certainly enough to keep you busy with trying certain races with different cars or just taking them for a spin. Not to mention that for every normal car in the game there is a cop car counterpart, with the addition of a couple! So if driving at 200+ MPH on a freeway with sirens on sounds fun to you, this game is for you. What about the handling then?

I personally enjoy how the cars handle. It is NOT a simulator in any way. It is arcade style racing with easy drifting so you can boost into those corners without losing tons of speed or control. To me it seems like all the cars handle in a very similar fashion, but I actually don't mind it. I don't think this type of racing is for everyone however, but it's not hard at all to get used to. Remember that this game is all about going fast to evade cops or bust racers using special abilities, so you can't be completely focused on realistic driving. But that brings me to another thing I love about this.

In the game, whether you are a racer or a cop, you have access to EMPs, spike strips, roadblocks, extreme turbo, and more. All these make the game more exciting and tense. If you are a racer, you can drop spike strips on cops OR other racers and use EMPs to pass someone, and if you are a cop, you use all of these to take down racers. I especially enjoyed the cop career more because it is really fun to smash into other cars and send them into a barrel roll or other cool crashes.

[b]NEUTRAL:[/b]

The free roam is one thing I always want in a racing game. Yes, Hot Pursuit does have it, but I feel that it is missing content. Being able to free roam as a racer, you would expect to occasionally run into a police car and get into some sort of epic chase, or vice versa being a cop, but sadly that just isn't the case. There aren't even any collectables! I guess the free roam in Hot Pursuit is pretty much there to test out cars or just go for a nice ride. So yes, it's nice to have, but it lacks content.

The menus are also sub-par. You can very easily tell that it is more suited for consoles. While I strongly recommend using a controller for this game anyways, the least they could have done was provide a more intuitive menu for the PC version.

[b]CONS:[/b]

With the exception of changing the color of the car, there is NO customization. I guess I "spoiled" myself with the feature of customizing back when I played on the PS2. I don't know why they ever took it out.

Now that I think about it, the menu tutorial at the very beginning of the game is pointless and [i]unskippable[/i]. It's like they expect you to know absolutely nothing about how a menu works. It takes a few minutes and is mandatory before actually playing the game.

[b]TL;DR:[/b]

NFS: Hot Pursuit is a really fun game with nice graphics, a great selection of cars, and tense racing. While free roam could have been significantly improved, it is always great to be able to go for a joyride in any of the vehicles you have unlocked, including the cop cars. Taking down racers or the police using EMPs, spike strips, roadblocks and more is very satisfying and really adds to the gameplay. There is no customization, with the exception of painting your car different colors, so this is a big let down, but nonetheless a very fun game. As a racing game enthusiast, I have to give this game a 7/10. Very fun!

One thing I have become increasingly frustrated with when playing racing games these past few years is that developers seem to throw more and more crap between you and actually racing with every new release. Hot Pursuit may well be the pinacle of this. 

The races themselves are a lot of fun. The cars have a good sense of speed, the sound is great, the crashes have impact and the game is very pretty all around. The problem is that you won't actually get to experience these things much. The majority of your time will be spent watching unskippable cutscenes, loading times, logging in on your EA account (with no way to save your login details so you don't have to enter them every singe time you start the game) or being harassed by the game to check out its totally cool social hub feature where it pretends to be Facebook. And God help you if the EA servers happen to be down, in which case the game will try connecting to them at the start of the game and the end of every single bloody 2 minute race, taking 10 seconds each time. It really adds up to the point where 50% of your time with Hot Pursuit is spent looking at shit you really don't want to see. 

Why can developers not understand that when someone buys a racing game, the chances are they actually want to race? No NFS, I don't give a shit about your unnecessary Facebook clone "feature", I don't want to try and connect to your instable servers every 2 seconds and I don't regard your variety of spinning wheels in loading screens or unskippable cutscenes with particular affection either. Please make them optional so I can drive some fast cars without jumping through a bajillion hoops for a 3 minute race. Thank you.

The Original Car Chase game, revamped... At least that's what I expected. Back in the '98 version it was a great fun game of racing vs your opponents, and the police - avoiding insanely high speed crashes and shaving that couple of seconds extra off a track, or getting a little nudge in at just the right moment, to win a race.

Fast-Forward many generations of game development and hardware cycles, and we have the reboot. 

Initially it looks promising, graphically it's a lot nicer, the tracks are interesting, and they've kept the tradition of high-risk shortcuts to get to the end faster - but this is one of the things that shows up the games truly hideous faults.

1- The enemies are scripted to keep up, not actually racing around the track as they look, but constantly teleporting around the track to be close to you. No matter how good you are, you cannot get more than a few seconds lead, even on a car you just saw crash into a virtually impossible situation, while you are at max boost - he'll be on your tail and overtaking the instant you take a corner less than optimally.

2- Speaking of cornering - it cannot be done without a horrible skid mechanic. You just dont get to keep control of the car. At the time the game was made, drifting was very trendy, and the makers seem to have decided to make it mandatory for every car, every race.

3- The collision detection is horrible for such a high end racing game. Often you pass another vehicle, or other obsticle, knowing you've cut it close, but also knowing you've missed, when suddenly the game decides you've hit, and not just clipped something, but catastrophically flipped your car and ruined your race.

4- Hardware support. After a few months of having this game, my nephew loved playing it for fun, so despite not being able to forgive it's foibles, I kept the game, but after I changed some stuff on my system, it's refused to run ever since. Gets to the loading screen, CTD with no error report.

RIP NFS memories.

A detailed review of:

Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit

Disclaimer:

Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit is a fantastic game. But I suggest you TO NOT buy the remastered version.
It's EA's greedy attempt at charging 30$ for a half-baked remaster. I don't see a reason to buy it, other than only for online play.
The remaster only has redone textures, added 2-5 at most new cars, doesn't have an unlocked framerate, and doesn't support high refresh rate monitors.
That makes the remastered version appear like a CTRL + C; CTRL + V with the normal one.
But if you can somehow buy the original, do it.

I'm going to start with the best of the game and progress to the worse.

Mechanics:

In this game, you can literally accelerate, brake, drift, use nitro... Take WHOLE minute saving off of a race shortcut, do hard maneuvers that feel rewarding, have a totally broken and aggressive at times, but also fun cop/racer enemy system... And I am not done.
In specific racing/cop events, you can use one of the most simple yet good mechanics.
Getting to place spike strips, summon helicopters, place roadblocks, use ridiculous nitro that can get you to top speed in 10 seconds, shoot an invisible signal to neutralize cars (EMP), and IM NOT DONE.
The most fun part is that you can wreck any enemy car near you, almost whenever you want.
The feeling of crushing and totaling the car in 1st place or was aggressive at you feels great.

10/10


Progression:

This game has a very linear progression, divided into two.
Cops and Racers. With lots, and I mean LOTS of events. And you can play both.
But even if it's linear, it doesn't mean that it's shallow content-wise. You have about 5 kinds of races/cop pursuits, including time trials. And they're divided, once again, into three leagues:
Sport, Super, Hyper
With each one, your cars get better and faster.
To progress quickly and easily, you have to get gold medals or distinctions in every race. That way you can guarantee that you will get the best cars.
For some people, the game may get repetitive later on. But with over 20 maps to race on, different car events, that likely won't happen.
That is the only real disadvantage to the progression. It may get boring. But 99% of the time, that isn't happening.
I should also mention that it may take 50 to 150 hours to finish the game at 100% without completing the online challenges. It depends on how fast you are.

9/10

Graphics:

If you have bought the game and haven't touched it or forgotten about it, and at least have a low-end gaming pc from 2017. Go now and play the game on 4K, heck. Even try ReShade (Google it) if you're into it and have an even better PC.
It's very, VERY easy to run on almost anything. It even runs great on most office computers. Yeah, I am not joking, because the game was made in...
Uhm... 2010
Don't let this be a turnoff. If you play the game on a decent monitor or TV, in 4K, with a controller, with a keyboard, with ReShade, or just on an ordinary computer with an average monitor, it will look good. It will look like a game that isn't old at all.
Need for Speed: Hot Pursuit is one of the best graphically aged games, in the fact that it still looks GREAT.
That still doesn't fix the other things that cannot be made better with ReShade or upscaling.
Because of that, the game looks "messy" in some areas but is absolutely amazing most of the time.

8/10

Sound:

The sounds for cars were pretty good. Everything from engine sounds to crashes, and even cop cars flying over the hood of my cars feel great and alive.
There isn't much else to say about the audio.
At the very least, because it's an old game.
It has better car sounds than Forza Horizon 4 :)

10/10

Story:
It's pretty much non-existent, as far as I know. I've always skipped cutscenes, so...
I guess the story is to become the "Most Wanted" and the best cop.
Because of what I said up above, I won't judge this category. I apologize for this.

??/??

Online Play:

It has an inactive community, as you have probably guessed. It might've been active a long time ago, but unfortunately, not now.
That's why the remaster exists. I hate to say this, the remaster is better in the area, because it's newer.

1/10

(10+10+9+8)/4=
~10/10 (9.25)

Score: (If online play matters a lot to you.)

(10+10+9+8+1)/5=
~8/10 (7.6)

If you value online play, consider your options and buy the remaster on a Steam Sale of at least 50% or more. If you don't care about online functionality, work some way out to buy the original on Steam.

I just want people to like this game just as much as I do, but if you don't, that's fine.

[h1]Need For Speed: Hot Pursuit[/h1]

[h1]Introduction[/h1]

Need For Speed has been one of those games that have been involved in my childhood to the present day to today, I still don't have any sense to give up on playing any of them. The Need For Speed Series for sure has been stuck with us since the very beginning since the release of [i]The Need for Speed (1994).[/i] Sure, I wasn't born at the time, but I still had a passionate playing it on my Fathers 1998 Gateway back in the days, including [i]Need For Speed III[/i] and [i]Porsche Unleashed[/i]. To put this in perspective, I played all of them and loved them, if [i]Need For Speed: Most Wanted (2005)[/i] were on the Steam Store I would instantly write a review of it on expressing how much I loved it. Need For Speed: Hot Pursuit was a game that I didn't expect much from, of course, I was still Semi-Young at the time, I would play anything honestly. I racked up at least 70+ if not more hours on my PS3.  All I have to say it was worth it...all of it, including today. 

Below I'll try my best to provide the information that will be needed if you're interested in purchasing this game, pointing out the Pros and Con's of what to expect and explaining the concept.

[h1]What is Need For Speed: Hot Pursuit?[/h1]

If you have played any of the Need For Speed's or take a look at the title, you can see it's involved with cars. [i]Fast ones...[/i] Criterion, which was known for the [i]Burnout[/i] series got involved this time, and I can see what they did, giving the crashes a 'Burnout Style' approach. It's not like Burnout, but you can see a pinch of the resemblance.  Imagine this game like cops and robbers. You the 'Racers' will be the Robbers and the 'Cops' are well...the cops. You race to point A to point B with a consistent pressure with cops gaining on you with 'Powers' or 'Gadgets'. Yes, this was a complete game changer for me and quite of few others. For some examples, you can EMP charge your opponents disabling them briefly and deploy spikestreaps behind you while you're blasting down the road at high speeds.

[h1]The Pro's[/h1]

[b]Vehicles/Progression[/b]

There's a great wide of Vehicle selections, you start off with a Low-Tier class or known as [i]Sports Series[/i]. Then you make your way up, fleeing away from cops and doing races to the Top-Tier class of [i]Hyper Series[/i]. This both applies between Racer and Cop modes. 

You start off basically unnoticed, then make your way as the Elite member of the Police Department. Otherwise being the racer, you make your way as the Most Wanted. The more you race and win, completing Challenges will boost your rep on what side you choose to take, it's all up to you on how you want to play it.

[b]The Gameplay[/b]

To me, the Gameplay handled well. You start off small, then you progress more and meet more challenging races to complete. Oh yeah, and better cars! 

You typically have your Standard Races where all you have is just Racers with no cops involved. Then you have Hot Pursuit, you race while you have the heat behind you with Police Cars gaining up on you with brute force. For the cops, you also get involved with the Racers and have to bust them before they reach the finish. The intercept mode is basically the same thing, but have to bust someone before the timer runs out for specific medals.

The transition of the map you have to race on [i]Seacrest County[/i] is great! You have your standard backroads and Highways that will cross through Wilderness's and mountains, then through the scorching desert and to the Coastline. The weather and time also is a neat feature. You'll see yourself racing through the nice mild/sunny weather as it slowly starts storming. Racing on the coastline is quite beautiful too as the sun sets on the horizon as it get's darker out. These little features are what I love, it was great back in 2010! [i]Understanding it's 2017, writing this like I'm in 2010 for some reason[/i]

The Gadget's that are given to you are also cool, you have EMP's, Turbo's, and SpikeStrips to deploy while in certain races, especially in Hot Pursuit. Both Racers and Cops have their own gadgets. For Cops, they can deploy Roadblocks and Helicopters on you, meanwhile, Racers can use Jammers to block communication and deploy the Turbo for a quick and brief getaway. 

The music is pretty great too especially the loading and main menu. Just hearing 30 Seconds To Mars in the introduction always got my hyped while hearing the police sirens in the background.

The sounds are just..perfect. 

[h1]The Con's[/h1]

Unfortunately, there isn't a lot of 'Perfect Games' if not at all, there's some flaw's that I feel like I need to point out.

There's, unfortunately, any StoryMode, although I would like one, it's not like the old Need For Speed Titles. But the cutscenes usually make up for it I suppose? To be fair, I just want to drive fast cars and if you're like me, I don't really think there would be a problem.

Freemode is rather limited, you can't set the time of day at all, but you do get the option to pick any car you want. Just be aware that there's no Cops or other Racers there, it's just you and the Civilian Vehicle AI's.

No DLC at all, PS3 and Xbox has them, but unfortunately, PC does not. I do know that there were some methods online to 'Download' them in, but I have not tried this myself and cannot confirm if it works or not. So I won't be any help on that.

Multiplayer, unfortunately, is dead on PC, it's a shame really. A lot of my hours on PS3 was online multiplayer based, you would be lucky to find a full room on PC some day. I still have yet to find somebody else.

[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]

If you want a racing game that's intense and fast-paced with an Arcade feel, I would suggest picking this up, full price or on Sale, it'll be worth your money. It's a game from 2010, a game that actually feels complete. [i]In my opinion[/i]. The music fit's well to me, the sounds are just right and there's a decent amount of car selections. The leveling up system isn't quite bad either, although can take awhile to complete, that's good. It's not too short and too long. Multiplayer is great as long as you buddy up with someone or hope to god you run into people. Personally, I like the new Power System or 'Gadgets' that got introduced, it didn't rather feel unbalanced to me, overall was a neat new feature that got put in. Just replaying this in 60FPS with better image quality is a refresh feel to me.

The awards from this game were well earned back in 2010, just hope someday I'll run into a populated server one day for Multiplayer?

I would personally recommend the game.

It's got everything arcadey that any other NFS game has. 

Physics? Non-existent. You're basically driving a huge box of concrete, which rides very weirdly. If you start accelerating very slowly and smoothly from a standstill, the engine immediately starts shaking the car like crazy, even though you're not doing any burnouts at 1 mph. Also, the car never stops by itself if you let off the gas, it just automatically keeps a 8-10 mph speed and cruises around. Why? No one knows, but cars with manual transmission don't work like that in real life.

Skill-based racing? Come again? It can hardly even be called "racing" per se as it's nothing more than a gamble. In a 12-mile race the only bit that matters is the last mile, more or less, because however good you drive in the first 11 miles is irrelevant. The rubber-banding in NFSHP is the worst I've ever seen, even by NFS standards - you can drive absolutely brilliantly without any hiccups and the NPCs will always be right behind you or one step ahead. You can literally see at the bottom of the minimap how spun-out racers and cops you leave behind immediately reset facing the correct direction with an initial speed that's higher than the one you're doing, even if you're going full-speed!! Need For Speed goes back to it's roots, before the era of Underground and it's sequels with Hot Pursuit, a arcade racing game developed by Criterion Games and published by Electronic Arts, in which you will join the war between races and cops filled with high speed police chases and exotic cars. Which side you will join?

Hot Pursuit is set in fictional Seacrest Country based on California, a USA state, and features over 160 km of open roads!
It's a paradise for races and their machines, but local police department, known as SCPD, dosen't like that, and will do everything to stop racing once and for all, spending money on fastest and most exotic machines in the world.

Game allows you to play as racers and cops, with each side having it's own career mode.
As a racer, you will compete in races with other drivers, try to survive chases with police, and climb your way up the ranks to become The Most Wanted.
You have few event types. From typical race, which involves you and other drivers only, through Time Attack where you will need to get to a point in shortest amount of time, to Hot Pursuit, which involves your not-so-friendly SCPD trying to bust you down while you will have to survive their attacks and win a race. 
Racing is what you did past 15 other NFS titles, so this racer career shouldn't suprise you. 
It has enough variety and balance between normal time attacks/racers and cop chases, and it still is really fun.

But you should be more interested in second career, a cop one, as this returns after 8 years, since that's how long it took to make a new Hot Pursuit game!
Starting as a rookie, you will bust racers and respond to dispatches to slowly climb up into ranks of SCPD, getting access to better, faster cars.
Again, you have few types of events for them. From responding to dispatches in time attacks, where every crash will give you penalty, to busting racers, sometimes only one, sometimes a whole race.

To help you survive cops, or to bust racers, you have power-ups!
Both sides have spikes, that can be dropped behind vehicles, and IEM, to stun and damage your opponents.
Races also have radar jamming, which will jam communication of cops and disallow them to use powerups, giving you a  short break, and turbo, which will give you a really big speed boost when nitro is not enough, but I recommend using it on straight road.
Cops can call and make a roadblock ahead that will damage and crash racers, allowing you to bust them, and call helicopter to tail a racer and drop spikes ahead of them.

Driving is arcade styled, but not as in games like Burnout.
Still, sliding on basically every turn and easy handling of cars allows you to have a lot of fun, especially on roads that are made for this type of driving.

Game also has a really big variety of cars!
There is around 70 cars in game, and are seperated into 5 ranked tiers, by progressing in the game you unlock next tiers and cars. And as in other HP games, the only customization you have in a game is color change, and only on racer side. 
Cops have special police livery. To be fair, I enjoy that for some reason. It's simple, allows you to simply use cars as cars.
And this is something related to original Hot Pursuit games, I love that they keep it up! 
Also as a fun fact, traffic cars are real, not unbraned, fictional models! Little detail that needs to be mentioned.

Game has other modes. A free roam mode, in which you can take a tour of Secrest Country, but without anything to do expect enjoying the views and music, and a photo mode, to show off your photographic skills.

There is Multiplayer, which has events type taken from game. It's fun, but hard to find people nowadays.

Cars sound great, but from sound design, soundtrack shines the most. I can safely say, this is the best soundtrack from Need For Speed games, period. Perfectly build for racing. Rest like some voice lines and the rest, is just..okay.

Game works great. No crashes, bugs, FPS drops, no nothing. 

The only problem with a game I could find is no DLC content to buy on Steam, as game has 3 DLC's that give you more races and vehicles. Shame.

Overall 2010 Need For Speed is a great game, successful return of Hot Pursuit. 
Both careers are enjoyable, including amazing soundtrack, power-ups that make a game more interesting, and a fun, arcade driving. 
8/10!

TL;DR version:  Good, wholesome arcade racing fun buried under in-game advertisements, unwieldy social systems, clunky menus and unskippable cutscenes.  Not worth buying even on sale (and I mean really on sale, $5 or less), unless you're very patient and don't have any better options available.

Long version:  So, Criterion did the actual legwork on this game, which means the arcade racing is easy to pick up and fun to play with, the cars are pleasingly slippery through the corners and the crashes are spectacular.  The pursuit gameplay is basically just the races, only you've got lights on your car and the objective is to smash the other cars to bits rather than reach the line.  Over time various tools are added to amp up both races and pursuits, allowing you to foil tailgaters with spike strips, screw over those ahead of you with EMP blasts, and other fun things.  Said tools get upgraded and you unlock new vehicles as you rack up points for wins and completing time trial challenges.  So far, so Burnout.

Really, there's absolutely nothing wrong with the core gameplay on display here, and I'd love to end the review and tell you to rush out and buy it.  It's an arcade racer by Criterion, of course it's good.  Unfortunately, it's been published by EA, which means there's a very large amount of unwieldy and unnecessary cruft not just weighing down the gameplay, but actively trying to prevent you from playing at all.

Let's just walk through what happens every time you boot this game.  First, you're presented with an unskippable corporate logo animation.  Then, you're presented with another unskippable corporate logo animation.  Then you get an unskippable static image of several corporate logos and some legal text.  Then there's an unskippable animation introducing the title screen.  Finally you can press a button to proceed to the main menu - except first you have to get past the "Autolog" (social gaming feature) login screen.  You're not required to create an account, but they do their very best to convince you otherwise.  Once you find the "cancel" button there, you're treated to an unskippable splash image advertising Need For Speed World, an MMO which was cancelled in 2015.  Finally, after several minutes of wasting your time and advertising at you, you are deposited in the main menu.

It gets better.  Or worse, I suppose, is more accurate:  The FIRST time you load the game, and the first time you access any feature, you're treated to a long, fully voiced, completely unskippable movie explaining what the feature does in exhaustive detail.   So the first time you load the game, you not only have to sit through several minutes of corporate logos and literal advertisements, you also need to suffer through 5+ minutes of being treated like a child who can't figure out what the shiny buttons on the menus do.

Furthermore, every time you unlock a new car, or tool/weapon, or upgrade for a tool/weapon, or "rank up" your police or racer profile, you're forced to sit through yet more unskippable cutscenes as they loudly and lengthily tell you that you can now drop two spike strips at once or that you've now got THREE chevrons on your virtual profile.  A simple text box of "Spike Strips updated: Can now drop double strips" would do perfectly fine, but instead you get to wait through a full minute of animated guff pretending that there's a manufacturer making these items for you and here's how they work and here's some diagrams of them in action and I'D LIKE TO PLAY THE NEXT RACE NOW, PLEASE.

It is, in summation, a game which does not respect your time, published by a company that sees you only as a wallet to advertise their other products to.  It fritters away your free time in dribs and drabs, taking several minutes to get you to the main menu, stealing away 30-90 seconds here and there to introduce new things in unnecessarily lengthy cutscenes, and chomping away 5 minutes or more the first time you access any feature or menu option to explain it in patronizing detail.  I bought this game on sale for something like $4, and I feel ripped off.

Criterion made a solid game. They really did.  It's nothing spectacular, but there's also nothing wrong with it.  All the problems lay in the unskippable cutscenes, the unskippable logos, the unskippable advertisements.  It drains away all the fun and engagement and leaves nothing.   I haven't played the game for weeks, and I don't see myself going back.  There are better arcade racers out there that won't waste your time. Buy them instead.

If you've played Need for Speed 3: Hot Pursuit and enjoyed that game, then feel free to just continue enjoying that gem from 1998. This game is just a test of your patience and a very poor followup that misses the point of "Hot Pursuit".

Graphically, the game looks great and the featured cars are modeled well. Playing the game as a cop is fun. Um, that's about it.

The first thing that you are treated to are some unskippable logos followed by some unskippable video sequences before you can start the game... or so you think. This is immediately followed by EA's Autolog online connectivity feature hassling you to log on with your EA Account credentials. While I have an EA account and Autolog acknowledged that it recognized my provided email address, no password that I have ever used in the past worked. So I decided to go ahead and make a new account. For whatever reason, Autolog accepted my email address, but never asked for a password to be provided and won't allow me to log on. Maybe the Autolog servers are offline? Some users say that they are still online, but just notoriously unstable. In any case, I get bugged about logging on every time I start the game. Several features of the game that have no business being tied to Autolog like "Photo Mode" refuse to allow me access because I'm not logged on.

After the Autolog harassment you can finally start the game. No, wait! Now you must watch an unskippable video. In fact any time you unlock a new tier of cars or new equipment you get an unskippable video. NFS:HP(2010) loves to slow you down at every opportunity. When it's not a video, it's the game's UI slowly adding up your points at the end of a race (partially skippable) or informing you that you've unlocked a new car (unskippable) or have gone up in wanted level (completely pointless and unskippable).

As for the actual racing, the one race type that really sticks out is Time Trial. Not because it's any good, but because nearly half of the races in the game are Time Trials. These races are by far the most boring as you just race from point A to point B by yourself under a set time limit. Preview is another race type, but don't let it fool you. It's just Time Trial with a car you haven't yet unlocked. If you avoid doing these terrible races, eventually they'll pile up and you won't be able to unlock any more fun races until you do the Time Trials and Previews.

The cars are split up into performance tiers. This has the side effect of preventing you from being able to choose a car from a different tier. Have you come to love a car or want an increased challenge by driving a slower car? Too bad. You have to pick a car from this race's arbitrary tier level. Many races even force you to drive a specific car.

The various gadgets in this game are fun to use, but are only available in Hot Pursuit. It would certainly be nice to have them in Race or especially Duel.

Oh yeah. This is a racing game, right? Where's the replay function after a race? I've had some awesome close calls and come from behind wins in this game, but when the race is done then that's it. No option to review your race or save the replay or anything. NFS3:HP(1998) let you do this. This would have been great in the age of Youtube and online connectivity to watch some awesome race replays.

Quickrace was a really nice feature in NFS3:HP(1998) that let you pick a track, difficulty, weather conditions, daylight conditions, number of opponents, and what cars they drive. Wanna race a bunch of Diablos while you drive a 'Vette? Go ahead. When you finally pull off a 1st place win, you could even save the replay! (Amazing!)

In short, this is a game that disappoints and tests your patience more than anything. It's irony of an artistic sort that this is a racing game with "speed" in the title that keeps you away from racing and having fun with with unnecessary features like Autolog, unskippable videos, and slowly advancing UI screens. If you ignore my review, then at least play through as a cop, though even the cop playthrough still has stupid Time Trials in the form of "Rapid Response".

It was about ten races in when I felt a strange sense of deja vu, as if I had raced these tracks before. And then it hit me; I had - back in 1998. This wasn't just another Need For Speed game branded with the name of one of the more popular iterations of the series; it was a remake! 

Now, you have to understand; I loved the 1998 "Hot Pursuit" (aka Need for Speed III); released 16 years ago, it remains one of my favorite racing titles (it was /the/ favorite until Porsche Unleashed unseated it two years later). Its great levels, solid driving, stylish cars and kick-ass soundtrack combined into an overall awesome package. Few of the later games in the Need For Speed franchise even approached the heights achieved by NFS3. But aging graphics and finicky hardware requirements meant it was increasingly difficult to relive the original experience. So when I started recognizing some familiar curves and sets in the 2011 remake, I got understandably excited.

Not that the 2011 Hot Pursuit is a 1-to-1 remake; it's more of an homage, utilizing many of the familiar tracks but updated with modern graphics and an open world. Still, it's a glorious return to an era of Lambroghini's and Porsches squealing unsafely around hairpin curves on gorgeous mountain and desert tracks. The car handling is wonderful; not in the least bit realistic, of course (I call it "pinball racing" for a reason!) but it feels very solid. The tracks are varied and beautiful, with a nice mix of curves and straight-aways, with numerous shortcuts to add some variety. 

But sadly, for every step forward the game makes a grievous step back. Worst of all is the AI, which is so tightly rubber-banded to the player as to remove all sense of challenge or achievement. How bad is it? Even when I cheated and disabled the AI entirely, my opponents were never further back than two seconds behind me. I never felt as if my skills were being fairly tested because there was never any distance between myself and the AI. It absolutely ruined the single-player experience. Almost as bad is how pushy EA is with their "Autolog" online service, without which a good three-quarters of the game is non-functional. I have no interest in the so-called "social" aspects of racing, but I'd have liked to check my race stats without having first create an account for yet another online service. Other missteps include an over-reliance on beat-the-clock races, a completely pointless free-roam mode, unskippable movies and an unbearable soundtrack. 

All in all, the 2011 Need For Speed Hot Pursuit has the seeds of greatness - varied tracks, good driving, beautiful cars - and it kept me entertained throughout its single-player missions. But it erred in too many other areas for it to be considered as one of the highpoints of the franchise.

The best [i]Need for Speed[/i] since [i]Carbon.[/i] Delightful visuals, ridiculously fun multiplayer, a gratifying level up system, and really pleasant driving mechanics. The game lets you take control of whatever side you want, the racers or the cops. Best part is that the chases are exhilarating from both perspectives. You're constantly unlocking things on this game, whether it is a car, a weapon upgrade, a milestone, or whatever, it keeps rewarding you. The prodigious amount of gorgeous and exotic cars are a pleasure to drive, accompanied by the fitting soundtrack. 

This game is not without flaws, however. If I was asked to define Autolog in one word, it would be [b]crap.[/b] Connection problems are common with it, and its lack of support is disruptive. A minor complaint of mine is that there is no actual story mode, it's just a lot of random racing. It's not exactly an issue, I just think a single-player story could've made the game significantly more interesting. Either way, this game is immense entertainment all around, if you can grab it and play it with some friends, I'm sure you will not be dissatisfied! Very nice job, Criterion. [b]8.5/10.0[/b]
